docs.title: Image Preprocessing Detector
docs.text: Welcome to the Image Preprocessing Detector documentation. This system intelligently analyzes documents (PDFs, images) and identifies required preprocessing steps before vector database ingestion for RAG applications.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Text Detection Gate: Fast routing to specialized processing paths
  • Classical Computer Vision: Skew, blur, contrast, and noise detection
  • Deep Learning: YOLOv8 layout detection and ML-based image quality assessment
  • Hybrid IQA: Per-element quality assessment for embedded images in documents
  • Correction Pipeline: OpenCV-based corrections with guardrails
  • JSON Output: COCO-aligned metadata for downstream processors

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Install the package:

pip install image-preprocessing-detector

Process a document:

imgprep process input.pdf --output result.json

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The system uses a multi-stage pipeline with text detection fork:

PDF/Image Input → Ingestion (300 DPI) → Text Gate
                                           ↓         ↓
                                      [NO TEXT]  [TEXT]
                                           ↓         ↓
                                   Classical IQA  YOLOv8 Layout
                                           ↓         ↓
                                      Correction Pipeline
                                           ↓
                                      JSON Output

docs.title: Upscaling Algorithms
docs.text:
Five OpenCV algorithms available:

  1. lanczos - Best quality (recommended for production)
  2. bicubic - Balanced speed/quality (development)
  3. inter_linear - Fastest (performance-critical)
  4. inter_cubic - Alternative high-quality
  5. inter_area - Downsampling (for oversized images)

docs.title: What The Diff PR Summaries Runbook
docs.text: Project: Image Preprocessing Detector Last Updated: 2025-11-06

docs.title: 📖 Overview
docs.text:
What The Diff (WTD) automatically generates AI-powered summaries for every pull request in the image_detection repository. These summaries provide reviewers with a quick, high-level overview of changes, reducing cognitive load and accelerating the review process.

Key Benefits: - Faster Reviews: Immediate understanding of PR scope and impact - Consistency: Standardized summaries across all PRs - Context Preservation: Captures intent and reasoning from code changes - Onboarding: Helps new contributors understand project evolution

docs.title: Integration Approach
docs.text: This project uses the shortcode method for WTD integration: - PR descriptions include wtd:summary placeholder - What The Diff replaces placeholder with AI-generated content - Integrated with mcp__zen-core__pr_prepare tool (see CLAUDE.md) - Automatic inclusion controlled by include_wtd parameter (default: true)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Repository admin access to image_detection on GitHub
  • GitHub account with authorization to install apps

docs.title: Installation Steps
docs.text:
1. Login to What The Diff
  2. Navigate to whatthediff.ai
  3. Click "Sign in with GitHub"

  4. Authorize the application

  5. Grant Repository Access

  6. In the What The Diff dashboard, navigate to "Repositories"
  7. Locate image_detection (or your organization's repository)

  8. Click "Enable" to activate WTD for this repo

  9. Configure Repository Settings

  10. Click on the enabled repository to access settings
  11. Configure according to recommendations below

docs.title: Operational Mode
docs.text:
Recommended: Use Pull Request Descriptions with shortcodes

## Summary
wtd:summary

## Test Plan
- [ ] Unit tests pass
- [ ] Integration tests pass
- [ ] Coverage maintained above 80%

Alternative: AI Comments (auto-posted to PRs) - Enable if team prefers comment-based summaries - Configure trigger: "On PR creation and updates"

docs.text:
• Default: 50,000 tokens per PR
  • Typical Usage: 2,000-8,000 tokens for Python ML projects
  • Recommendation: Keep default unless hitting limits on large refactors

docs.title: PR Preparation with Zen MCP
docs.text:
The project uses the mcp__zen-core__pr_prepare tool to automate PR creation with WTD integration:

# Claude Code automatically invokes:
mcp__zen-core__pr_prepare --include_wtd=true --target_branch=main

What happens: 1. Tool analyzes git commit history and changes 2. Generates PR title and body with context 3. Inserts wtd:summary shortcode in PR description 4. Pushes branch and creates draft PR on GitHub 5. What The Diff detects shortcode and generates summary 6. Summary appears inline within minutes

docs.text:

Important: Place wtd:summary before detailed change descriptions to avoid duplicate content.

docs.title: Trigger Phase
docs.text:
What The Diff activates when: - Pull request is opened - Pull request is reopened - New commits are pushed to an open PR

Exclusions: - Bot-authored PRs (dependabot, renovate, github-actions) - Draft PRs (if configured in settings)

docs.title: Diff Analysis
docs.text:
1. Fetch Changes: WTD retrieves the PR diff from GitHub API
  2. Apply Filters: Excludes files matching configured patterns (see File Exclusion Patterns)
  3. Token Estimation: Calculates token usage based on remaining diff
  4. Context Building: Includes commit messages, file paths, and code context

docs.title: Summary Generation
docs.text:
1. AI Processing: Sends filtered diff to OpenAI GPT-4 or Claude API
  2. Summary Creation: Generates:
  3. High-level overview (1-2 sentences)
  4. Key changes by module/category
  5. Potential impact areas
  6. Testing recommendations (if applicable)
  7. Shortcode Replacement: Injects summary into PR description where wtd:summary appears

Typical Latency: 30-90 seconds for Python ML projects with 500-2000 LOC changes

# Test coverage reports

Note: This project's .gitignore already excludes most generated files, so .gitattributes is optional but recommended for any committed artifacts.

docs.title: Summary Not Appearing
docs.text:
Symptom: PR created but no WTD summary generated

Checks: 1. Verify wtd:summary shortcode is present in PR description 2. Check repository is enabled in What The Diff dashboard 3. Confirm PR is not from a bot account (dependabot, renovate) 4. Check What The Diff status page for service issues

Resolution: - Edit PR description to add/fix wtd:summary shortcode - Close and reopen PR to trigger regeneration - Check organization billing if on paid plan

docs.title: Token Limit Exceeded
docs.text:
Symptom: Summary incomplete or error message about token limits

Causes: - Large refactoring PRs (10,000+ LOC changes) - Binary files not properly excluded - Generated files included in diff

Resolution: 1. Review File Exclusion Patterns configuration 2. Add problematic file patterns to exclusion list 3. Split large PRs into smaller, focused changes 4. Increase token limit in What The Diff settings (if available)

docs.title: Incorrect or Low-Quality Summary
docs.text:
Symptom: Summary misses key changes or includes irrelevant details

Causes: - Inadequate commit messages (WTD uses these for context) - Complex architectural changes without documentation - Mixed concerns in single PR (features + refactoring + fixes)

Resolution: 1. Write descriptive commit messages following Conventional Commits format 2. Add context in PR description above wtd:summary shortcode: 

## Context
This PR implements Phase 2 hybrid IQA approach, addressing the architectural
correction identified in ARCHITECTURE_CORRECTION.md.

## Summary
wtd:summary
3. Split PRs to focus on single concerns 4. Regenerate summary by editing/saving PR description

docs.title: WTD Dashboard Access Issues
docs.text:
Symptom: Cannot access What The Diff dashboard or settings

Resolution: - Verify GitHub organization admin privileges - Re-authorize What The Diff GitHub app - Check organization's third-party app policies - Contact What The Diff support: support@whatthediff.ai

docs.title: For PR Authors
docs.text:
1. Write Clear Commit Messages: WTD uses these for context 

    feat(detection): add YOLOv8 layout detection for text documents

- Implement LayoutDetector class with YOLOv8n inference
- Add bounding box extraction with COCO alignment
- Include confidence thresholding (default 0.5)

Relates to #42

  2. Use Shortcodes Strategically: Place wtd:summary early in PR description 

    ## Summary
wtd:summary

## Detailed Changes
[Your detailed notes here]

  3. Provide Context: Add brief context for complex changes 

    ## Context
Addresses architectural correction for hybrid IQA approach.
See ARCHITECTURE_CORRECTION.md for detailed rationale.

## Summary
wtd:summary

  4. Keep PRs Focused: Smaller, focused PRs generate better summaries

  5. Target: < 500 LOC changes per PR
  6. Single concern per PR (one feature, one fix, one refactor)

docs.title: For Reviewers
docs.text:
1. Read Summary First: Use WTD summary as PR overview before diving into code
  2. Validate Against Changes: Ensure summary accurately reflects actual changes
  3. Provide Feedback: If summary misses key points, add reviewer comments to supplement
  4. Trust but Verify: WTD is a tool, not a replacement for thorough review

docs.title: For Maintainers
docs.text:
1. Monitor Token Usage: Check What The Diff dashboard monthly for usage patterns
  2. Refine Exclusions: Add new patterns as project evolves (e.g., new build artifacts)
  3. Review Quality: Periodically assess summary quality and adjust settings
  4. Educate Team: Share this runbook with new contributors

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: This document provides reference documentation for the Image Preprocessing Detector's external interface.

docs.title: imgprep process
docs.text:
Process a document and detect preprocessing requirements.

Usage:

poetry run imgprep process INPUT [OPTIONS]

Arguments:

  • INPUT: Path to input PDF or image file

Options:

  • --output PATH, -o PATH: Output JSON file path (required)
  • --dry-run: Detection only, skip corrections (flag)
  • --blur-threshold FLOAT: Blur detection threshold 0.0-1.0 (default: 0.8)
  • --skew-threshold FLOAT: Skew detection threshold 0.0-1.0 (default: 0.7)
  • --contrast-threshold FLOAT: Contrast detection threshold 0.0-1.0 (default: 0.7)
  • --help: Show help message

Examples:

# Process single file and save to JSON
poetry run imgprep process input.pdf --output result.json

# Process with custom thresholds
poetry run imgprep process input.pdf --output result.json --blur-threshold 0.90 --skew-threshold 0.95

# Detection only (skip corrections)
poetry run imgprep process input.pdf --output result.json --dry-run

Output Format:

The command outputs JSON conforming to the DocumentMetadata schema. See JSON Schema section below.

docs.title: imgprep batch
docs.text:
Batch process multiple documents.

Usage:

poetry run imgprep batch INPUT_DIR OUTPUT_DIR [OPTIONS]

Arguments:

  • INPUT_DIR: Directory containing input PDF or image files
  • OUTPUT_DIR: Directory where results will be saved

Options:

  • --dry-run: Detection only, skip corrections (flag)
  • --blur-threshold FLOAT: Blur detection threshold 0.0-1.0 (default: 0.8)
  • --skew-threshold FLOAT: Skew detection threshold 0.0-1.0 (default: 0.7)
  • --contrast-threshold FLOAT: Contrast detection threshold 0.0-1.0 (default: 0.7)
  • --help: Show help message

Examples:

# Process all PDFs and images in a directory
poetry run imgprep batch input_dir/ output_dir/

# Batch process with dry-run
poetry run imgprep batch docs/ results/ --dry-run

# Batch process with custom thresholds
poetry run imgprep batch docs/ results/ --blur-threshold 0.9

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Currently, the primary interface is the CLI. The Python API provides schema validation:

from image_preprocessing_detector.schema import DocumentMetadata
from image_preprocessing_detector.utils import setup_logging, get_logger

# Setup logging
setup_logging(level="INFO", json_logs=False)
logger = get_logger(__name__)

# Use the CLI to generate output, then validate and load JSON
metadata = DocumentMetadata.from_json_file("output.json")
logger.info("Processed document", pages=metadata.num_pages)

Note: Direct Python processing API (process_document function) is planned for a future release and is not yet available. Use the CLI for document processing.

docs.title: Schema Validation
docs.text:
from image_preprocessing_detector.schema import (
    DetectedIssue,
    DocumentElement,
    PageMetadata,
    DocumentMetadata,
)

# Create metadata with validation
metadata = DocumentMetadata(
    source_file="document.pdf",
    num_pages=10,
    processing_version="0.1.0",
)

# Access page metadata
for page in metadata.pages:
    print(f"Page {page.page_number}: {len(page.detected_issues)} issues")

# Serialize to JSON
json_str = metadata.model_dump_json(indent=2)

# Deserialize from JSON
loaded_metadata = DocumentMetadata.model_validate_json(json_str)

docs.title: DocumentMetadata
docs.text:
Root metadata object for a processed document.

Fields:

  • document_id (str, required): Unique identifier for the document
  • file_name (str, required): Original filename
  • source_mime (str, required): Source MIME type (e.g., "application/pdf", "image/jpeg")
  • num_pages (int, required): Total number of pages (must be > 0)
  • processing_version (ProcessingVersion, required): Processing pipeline version information
  • pages (List[PageMetadata], required): Metadata for each page

Example:

{
  "document_id": "doc_123",
  "file_name": "document.pdf",
  "source_mime": "application/pdf",
  "num_pages": 5,
  "processing_version": {
    "pipeline_version": "0.1.0",
    "iqa_model_hash": null,
    "layout_model_hash": null,
    "thresholds": {
      "blur": 0.8,
      "skew": 0.7,
      "contrast": 0.7
    },
    "timestamp": "2025-11-07T12:00:00Z"
  },
  "pages": [...]
}

docs.title: PageMetadata
docs.text:
Metadata for a single page.

Fields:

  • page_index (int, required): Zero-based page index (must be >= 0)
  • width_px (int, required): Page width in pixels (must be > 0)
  • height_px (int, required): Page height in pixels (must be > 0)
  • dpi_input (int, required): Input DPI of the page (must be > 0)
  • dpi_effective (int, required): Effective DPI after processing (must be > 0)
  • detected_issues (List[DetectedIssue], optional): Page-level quality issues detected
  • planned_actions (List[PlannedAction], optional): Planned correction actions
  • elements (List[DocumentElement], optional): Detected document elements (tables, images, etc.)
  • languages (List[LanguageInfo], optional): Detected languages/scripts
  • transform_history (List[TransformHistory], optional): History of transformations applied

Example:

{
  "page_index": 0,
  "width_px": 2550,
  "height_px": 3300,
  "dpi_input": 300,
  "dpi_effective": 300,
  "detected_issues": [...],
  "planned_actions": [...],
  "elements": [...],
  "languages": [],
  "transform_history": []
}

docs.title: DetectedIssue
docs.text:
An image quality issue detected in the document.

Fields:

  • type (IssueType, required): Issue type enum value ("noise", "blur", "skew", "perspective", "low_contrast", "orientation", "low_dpi")
  • confidence (float, required): Detection confidence (0.0-1.0, validated)
  • severity (IssueSeverity, required): Severity level enum value ("low", "medium", "high", "critical")
  • metrics (dict, optional): Additional metrics specific to the issue type

Example:

{
  "type": "blur",
  "confidence": 0.92,
  "severity": "high",
  "metrics": {
    "laplacian_variance": 45.2,
    "threshold": 100.0
  }
}

docs.title: DocumentElement
docs.text:
A document element (table, image, handwriting, formula, text block, figure).

Fields:

  • id (str, required): Unique identifier for this element
  • category (ElementCategory, required): Category enum value ("table", "image", "handwriting", "formula", "text_block", "figure")
  • bbox (List[int], required): Bounding box in COCO format [x, y, width, height] (exactly 4 non-negative integers)
  • polygon (List[List[int]], optional): Optional polygon points for irregular shapes
  • confidence (float, required): Detection confidence (0.0-1.0, validated)
  • attributes (dict, optional): Additional attributes (script, handwriting_prob, etc.)
  • quality_issues (List[DetectedIssue], optional): Quality issues specific to this element (for hybrid IQA on embedded images)
  • needs_correction (bool, optional): Whether this element requires quality correction (default: false)
  • correction_applied (dict, optional): Details of correction applied to this element

Example:

{
  "id": "elem_001",
  "category": "table",
  "bbox": [100, 200, 800, 600],
  "polygon": null,
  "confidence": 0.95,
  "attributes": {
    "num_rows": 10,
    "num_cols": 5
  },
  "quality_issues": [],
  "needs_correction": false,
  "correction_applied": null
}

from image_preprocessing_detector.utils import setup_logging, get_logger

# Setup structured logging

    level="INFO",          # Log level

docs.title: Log Levels
docs.text:
• DEBUG: Detailed diagnostic information
  • INFO: Confirmation that things are working
  • WARNING: Indication of potential problems
  • ERROR: Serious problems that need attention
  • CRITICAL: Critical failures

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
The CLI provides clear error messages for common issues:

  • File not found: Clear message when input file doesn't exist
  • Invalid format: Warnings for unsupported file formats
  • Processing errors: Detailed error messages with suggestions

Use the --dry-run flag to validate inputs without performing corrections.

For Python API error handling, standard Python exceptions are raised:

from pathlib import Path

try:
    # Validate JSON output from CLI
    metadata = DocumentMetadata.from_json_file("output.json")
except FileNotFoundError:
    logger.error("Output file not found")
except Exception as e:
    logger.error("Failed to load metadata", error=str(e))

docs.title: Batch Processing
docs.text:
Use the CLI batch command to process multiple documents efficiently:

# Process entire directory
poetry run imgprep batch input_dir/ output_dir/

# The batch command automatically:
# - Finds all supported files (.pdf, .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .tiff)
# - Processes them sequentially
# - Saves results to individual JSON files in output directory

docs.title: Custom Thresholds
docs.text:
Adjust detection sensitivity using CLI options:

# More sensitive blur detection (higher threshold = more strict)
poetry run imgprep process input.pdf --output result.json --blur-threshold 0.9

# Less sensitive skew detection (lower threshold = more lenient)
poetry run imgprep process input.pdf --output result.json --skew-threshold 0.6

# Combine multiple thresholds
poetry run imgprep batch docs/ results/ \
  --blur-threshold 0.9 \
  --skew-threshold 0.8 \
  --contrast-threshold 0.75

docs.title: Transform History
docs.text:

# Access transform history
for transform in metadata.transform_history:
    print(f"{transform.transform_type}: {transform.parameters}")

# Check if specific transform was applied
has_deskew = any(
    t.transform_type == "deskew"
    for t in metadata.transform_history
)

# Security Policy

## Supported Versions

Currently supported versions for security updates:

| Version | Supported          |
| ------- | ------------------ |
| 0.1.x   | :white_check_mark: |

## Reporting a Vulnerability

**Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues.**

Instead, please report them via:

### GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting

Use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting feature:
https://github.com/williaby/image-preprocessing-detector/security/advisories/new

### Email

Alternatively, email security reports to: [your-email]

Include:
- Type of vulnerability
- Full path to affected source file(s)
- Location of affected code (tag/branch/commit)
- Step-by-step instructions to reproduce
- Proof-of-concept or exploit code (if possible)
- Impact assessment

## Response Timeline

- **Acknowledgment**: Within 7 days
- **Initial Assessment**: Within 14 days
- **Fix Timeline**:
  - Critical: Within 30 days
  - High: Within 60 days
  - Medium: Within 60 days
  - Low: Next release cycle

## Disclosure Policy

- Security advisories published after fix is available
- CVE requested for significant vulnerabilities
- Credit given to reporters (unless anonymity requested)

## Security Update Process

1. Fix developed in private fork
2. Fix tested and reviewed
3. Security advisory published
4. Patched version released
5. Public disclosure with CVE (if applicable)

## Security Best Practices for Users

- Keep dependencies updated: `poetry update`
- Run security scans: `poetry run bandit -r src`
- Check for known vulnerabilities: `poetry run safety check`
- Review security advisories: https://github.com/williaby/image-preprocessing-detector/security/advisories

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
docs.text: This directory contains Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for the Image Preprocessing Detector project.

docs.title: What is an ADR?
docs.text:
An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a document that captures an important architectural decision made along with its context and consequences. ADRs help us:

  • Understand why decisions were made
  • Track the evolution of the architecture
  • Onboard new team members
  • Avoid repeating past discussions
  • Learn from both good and bad decisions

docs.title: ADR Format
docs.text:
Each ADR follows this structure:

# ADR-NNN: [Title]

**Status**: [Proposed | Accepted | Deprecated | Superseded]
**Date**: YYYY-MM-DD
**Deciders**: [Names]
**Related**: [Links to related ADRs, issues, PRs]

## Context

What is the issue we're facing? What factors led to this decision?

## Decision

What did we decide to do?

## Consequences

### Positive

What are the benefits of this decision?

### Negative

What are the drawbacks or costs?

### Neutral

What are the neutral implications?

## Alternatives Considered

What other options did we evaluate and why were they rejected?

## References

Links to relevant documentation, discussions, or external resources.

docs.title: ADR-001: Consolidate Python Linting with Ruff
docs.text: Status: ✅ Accepted Date: 2025-01-08 Deciders: Byron Williams Related: Sprint 3 - Advanced Testing and Tooling Consolidation

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The project used multiple overlapping Python linting and formatting tools:

  • Black: Code formatting (line length, quotes, indentation)
  • Ruff: Limited linting (9 rule categories: E, W, F, I, B, C4, UP, ARG, SIM)
  • pydocstyle: Docstring style checking (Google convention)
  • MyPy: Type checking (strict on src/, relaxed on tests/)
  • interrogate: Docstring coverage metrics
  • Bandit: Security scanning

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. Tool Duplication: Black and Ruff formatter serve the same purpose
  2. Performance Overhead: Multiple tools running sequentially in pre-commit hooks
  3. Configuration Fragmentation: Settings spread across multiple tools
  4. Maintenance Burden: Keeping multiple tools updated and coordinated

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Maintain comprehensive code quality coverage
  • Preserve Google-style docstring enforcement
  • Keep security scanning capabilities
  • Maintain type checking rigor
  • Minimize pre-commit hook execution time

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Consolidate Black, pydocstyle, and partial Bandit functionality into Ruff.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text:
1. Replace Black with Ruff Format
  2. Enable [tool.ruff.format] in pyproject.toml
  3. Black-compatible formatting (88 char line length)

  4. Add ruff-format pre-commit hook

  5. Replace pydocstyle with Ruff D Rules

  6. Add "D" (pydocstyle) to Ruff lint rules
  7. Configure Google-style convention

  8. Remove standalone pydocstyle hook

  9. Supplement Bandit with Ruff S Rules

  10. Add "S" (flake8-bandit) for basic security checks
  11. Keep standalone Bandit for advanced security scanning

  12. Ruff catches common issues, Bandit for deep analysis

  13. Expand Ruff Linting

  14. From 9 to 13 rule categories

  15. Added: D (pydocstyle), S (security), N (naming), A (builtins), DTZ (datetime), PIE, Q (quotes), RET (return), PTH (pathlib)

  16. Keep Specialized Tools

  17. MyPy: Unique type checking capabilities
  18. interrogate: Coverage metrics and reporting
  19. Bandit: Advanced security pattern detection

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 88
target-version = "py312"

[tool.ruff.format]
quote-style = "double"
docstring-code-format = true

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "W", "F", "I", "B", "C4", "UP", "ARG", "SIM", "D", "S", "T20", "PT", "RUF", "N", "A", "DTZ", "PIE", "Q", "RET", "PTH"]

[tool.ruff.lint.pydocstyle]
convention = "google"

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
1. Single Formatter: Ruff format replaces Black (one less tool)
  2. Unified Configuration: All linting rules in one place
  3. Performance: Ruff is 10-100× faster than traditional tools
  4. Consistency: Single tool enforces multiple dimensions of code quality
  5. Maintenance: Fewer dependencies to update and coordinate
  6. Pre-commit Speed: Faster hook execution with fewer tools

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
1. Migration Effort: Required updating pre-commit hooks and CI workflows
  2. Learning Curve: Team needs to understand Ruff's unified approach
  3. Bandit Overlap: Some security rules now checked by both Ruff (S) and Bandit
  4. Mitigation: Acceptable redundancy, Bandit provides deeper analysis

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
1. Coverage Unchanged: All checks still enforced, just different tool
  2. Configuration Migration: Straightforward translation from old tools to Ruff

docs.title: Alternative 1: Keep All Tools Separate
docs.text: Rejected: Maintains tool duplication and slower pre-commit hooks

docs.title: Alternative 2: Remove MyPy and Use Only Ruff
docs.text: Rejected: Ruff doesn't do type checking, MyPy is essential for type safety

docs.title: Alternative 3: Remove Bandit and Use Only Ruff S Rules
docs.text: Rejected: Ruff's security rules are basic, Bandit catches advanced patterns

docs.title: Alternative 4: Adopt Pylint Instead of Ruff
docs.text: Rejected: Slower than Ruff, doesn't include formatting, heavier configuration

docs.title: ADR-002: Separate Mutation Testing from Main CI
docs.text: Status: ✅ Accepted Date: 2025-01-08 Deciders: Byron Williams Related: Sprint 3 - Advanced Testing and Tooling Consolidation

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Mutation testing is a powerful technique for assessing test quality by introducing small code changes (mutations) and verifying that tests catch them. However, mutation testing has significant performance implications:

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• Runtime: 10-100× slower than regular test suite
  • Cost: Expensive for large codebases (100+ mutations)
  • Diminishing Returns: Value comes from identifying weak tests, not real-time verification

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Test Quality: Need to verify tests catch mutations
  2. CI Performance: Main CI must remain fast (< 15 minutes)
  3. Actionable Feedback: Only flag when mutation score drops below threshold
  4. Cost Control: Avoid expensive operations on every commit

docs.title: User Request
docs.text: "I want mutmut to be separate in the workflows from the other tools so that it can be scheduled on its own cadence and only flag above a predefined threshold"

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Create dedicated mutation testing workflow running on weekly schedule with configurable thresholds.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
1. Separate Workflow: .github/workflows/mutation-testing.yml
  2. NOT part of main CI gates
  3. Does not block PRs

  4. Independent failure/success status

  5. Weekly Schedule: Sundays at 2:00 AM UTC

  6. Runs during low-activity period
  7. One execution per week reduces cost

  8. Manual trigger available for on-demand testing

  9. Threshold-Based Flagging: Default 80% mutation score

  10. Only fails if score drops below threshold
  11. Prevents false positives from edge case mutations

  12. Configurable via workflow_dispatch input

  13. Comprehensive Reporting:

  14. HTML report artifact (90-day retention)
  15. JSON results for programmatic analysis
  16. Automatic PR comments with mutation scores
  17. GitHub step summary with visual metrics

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
# Weekly schedule (Sundays 2:00 AM UTC)
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 2 * * 0"
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      mutation_threshold:
        default: '80'
        type: string

# pyproject.toml
[tool.mutmut]
paths_to_mutate = "src/"
runner = "poetry run pytest -x --assert=plain -o addopts=''"
tests_dir = "tests/"

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
1. Fast CI: Main CI remains < 15 minutes (no mutation testing overhead)
  2. Cost Control: Weekly execution vs. per-commit (saving ~95% of mutation runs)
  3. Actionable Alerts: Only flags real test quality issues (threshold-based)
  4. Comprehensive Analysis: Full mutation testing without time pressure
  5. Non-Blocking: Doesn't prevent merges, guides improvements
  6. Flexible Threshold: Adjustable via workflow_dispatch for different quality bars

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
1. Delayed Feedback: Issues discovered weekly vs. per-commit
  2. Mitigation: Manual workflow_dispatch available for on-demand testing
  3. Longer Runtime: 120-minute timeout for comprehensive testing
  4. Acceptable: Not blocking PRs, runs overnight
  5. Additional Workflow: One more workflow to maintain
  6. Minimal: Standard GitHub Actions patterns

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
1. Coverage vs. Speed Trade-off: Accepted for better overall velocity
  2. Separate Quality Signal: Mutation score tracked independently from coverage

docs.title: Alternative 1: Mutation Testing in Main CI
docs.text: Rejected: - Would add 30-60 minutes to PR feedback loop - Expensive for every commit - May block valid PRs on edge case mutations

docs.title: Alternative 2: Mutation Testing on Every PR
docs.text: Rejected: - Too expensive (cost scales with PR volume) - Slower PR velocity - Similar issues to Alternative 1

docs.title: Alternative 3: No Mutation Testing
docs.text: Rejected: - Misses opportunity to improve test quality - No mechanism to detect weak test coverage - Lower confidence in test suite effectiveness

docs.title: ADR-003: Adopt Property-Based Testing with Hypothesis
docs.text: Status: ✅ Accepted Date: 2025-01-08 Deciders: Byron Williams Related: Sprint 3 - Advanced Testing and Tooling Consolidation

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Traditional example-based testing (pytest) tests specific inputs and outputs. While effective, it has limitations:

docs.title: Limitations of Example-Based Testing
docs.text:
1. Limited Coverage: Only tests cases the developer thinks of
  2. Edge Case Blind Spots: May miss boundary conditions
  3. Maintenance: Each edge case requires a new test
  4. False Confidence: 100% coverage doesn't mean all behaviors tested

docs.title: Project Requirements
docs.text:
The Image Preprocessing Detector handles diverse inputs: - PDF files (various encodings, corrupted data) - Images (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, corrupted headers) - Bounding boxes (coordinates, dimensions) - Confidence scores (0.0-1.0 range validation) - Document metadata (JSON serialization/deserialization)

Need: Systematic way to discover edge cases and verify invariants across input space.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Adopt Hypothesis for property-based testing to complement example-based pytest tests.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
1. Complement, Don't Replace: Keep example-based tests for known scenarios
  2. Focus on Invariants: Test properties that should always hold
  3. Custom Strategies: Build domain-specific data generators
  4. Roundtrip Testing: Verify serialization/deserialization
  5. Boundary Validation: Test edge cases systematically

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Created tests/unit/test_property_based.py with:

  1. Custom Hypothesis Strategies: 

    @composite
def confidence_scores(draw):
    """Generate valid confidence scores (0.0 to 1.0)."""
    return draw(st.floats(min_value=0.0, max_value=1.0, allow_nan=False))

@composite
def bounding_boxes(draw):
    """Generate valid COCO-format bounding boxes [x, y, width, height]."""
    # ... ensures all coordinates and dimensions are positive

  2. Property Tests:

  3. Validation invariants: 0.0 <= confidence <= 1.0 always holds
  4. Roundtrip serialization: serialize(deserialize(x)) == x
  5. Format constraints: COCO bboxes always [x, y, width, height]
  6. Boundary conditions: Page dimensions must be positive

  7. Edge cases: Multi-page documents, empty metadata

  8. Integration with pytest: Hypothesis integrates seamlessly with existing test suite

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
@given(confidence_scores())
def test_confidence_always_in_valid_range(confidence: float) -> None:
    """Property: All generated confidence scores must be valid."""
    assert 0.0 <= confidence <= 1.0

    issue = DetectedIssue(
        type=IssueType.BLUR,
        confidence=confidence,
        severity=IssueSeverity.LOW,
    )
    assert issue.confidence == confidence

@given(detected_issues())
def test_detected_issue_json_roundtrip(issue: DetectedIssue) -> None:
    """Property: JSON encode → decode should preserve data."""
    json_str = issue.model_dump_json()
    deserialized = DetectedIssue.model_validate_json(json_str)

    assert deserialized.type == issue.type
    assert abs(deserialized.confidence - issue.confidence) < 1e-6

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
1. Edge Case Discovery: Hypothesis finds edge cases developers miss
  2. Example: Found datetime timezone handling issues during implementation
  3. Invariant Verification: Systematically tests properties that should always hold
  4. Reduced Test Maintenance: One property test replaces dozens of example tests
  5. Regression Prevention: Hypothesis saves failing examples for regression testing
  6. Documentation: Property tests document system invariants
  7. Confidence Boost: More confident in handling diverse real-world inputs

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
1. Learning Curve: Team needs to understand property-based testing concepts
  2. Mitigation: Created comprehensive examples in test_property_based.py
  3. Test Runtime: Hypothesis runs 100+ examples per test (slower than single example)
  4. Mitigation: Acceptable overhead (< 5 seconds per test class)
  5. Debugging: Shrinking failing examples can be complex
  6. Mitigation: Hypothesis provides minimal failing example automatically

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
1. Complementary Approach: Works alongside example-based tests
  2. Additional Dependency: Hypothesis already installed (0.21.0+)

docs.title: Alternative 1: Only Example-Based Testing
docs.text: Rejected: - Misses edge cases - Requires manual enumeration of test cases - Less confidence in handling diverse inputs

docs.title: Alternative 2: QuickCheck (Haskell-style)
docs.text: Rejected: - Hypothesis is the Python standard - Better pytest integration - More active Python community

docs.title: Alternative 3: Faker for Test Data
docs.text: Rejected: - Faker generates realistic data, not edge cases - Doesn't verify invariants - No automatic shrinking

docs.title: Alternative 4: Manual Fuzzing
docs.text: Rejected: - Less systematic than Hypothesis - No shrinking to minimal failing example - More code to maintain

docs.title: Test Coverage
docs.text:
Property-based tests added for:

  1. Schema Validation (5 properties):
  2. Confidence score ranges
  3. Bounding box format constraints
  4. Invalid input rejection
  5. Roundtrip serialization

  6. JSON encode/decode

  7. Transformations (2 properties):

  8. Transform history recording

  9. Multi-transform composition

  10. Edge Cases (3 properties):

  11. Page dimension validation
  12. Multi-page documents

  13. Empty/minimal metadata

  14. Integration (1 property):

  15. Quality issues serialization

docs.title: ADR-004: GitHub Actions Security Hardening
docs.text: Status: ✅ Accepted Date: 2025-01-08 Deciders: Byron Williams Related: Sprint 1 - Workflow Security Hardening, OpenSSF Scorecard Compliance

docs.title: Context
docs.text: OpenSSF Scorecard identified security issues in GitHub Actions workflows:

docs.title: Identified Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
1. Overly Permissive Tokens: Workflows had permissions: write-all or no explicit permissions
  2. Risk: Compromised workflow can modify code, publish releases, access secrets

  3. Impact: Supply chain attack vector

  4. Download-Then-Run Patterns: 7 instances of curl | python for Poetry installation 

    curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -

  5. Risk: MITM attack could inject malicious code

  6. Impact: Build-time code execution vulnerability

  7. Missing Action SHA Pinning: Some actions pinned by tag instead of SHA

  8. Risk: Tag can be moved to malicious commit
  9. Impact: Workflow compromise

docs.title: OpenSSF Scorecard Score
docs.text:
• Before: Token-Permissions: 0/10, Dangerous-Workflow: 3/10
  • Target: Token-Permissions: 10/10, Dangerous-Workflow: 10/10
  • Impact: Overall score improvement: ~6.8 → ~8.5 (+1.7 points)

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Implement comprehensive security hardening across all 9 GitHub Actions workflows.

docs.title: Changes
docs.text:
1. Least-Privilege Token Permissions
  2. Top-level: permissions: read-all (default deny)
  3. Job-level: Grant write permissions only where needed
permissions: read-all  # Top-level default

jobs:
  security-scan:
    permissions:
      security-events: write  # Only for SARIF upload
      contents: read
  1. Eliminate Download-Then-Run Patterns
  2. Replace curl | python with trusted GitHub Actions
  3. Use SHA-pinned snok/install-poetry@76e04a911780d5b312d89783f7b1cd627778900a (v1.4.1)

  4. Add POETRY_VERSION: 2.1.2 environment variable for consistency

  5. Complete SHA Pinning

  6. All actions pinned by commit SHA with version comment
  7. Example: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2

docs.title: Affected Workflows
docs.text: Workflow Permissions Poetry Pattern Impact ci.yml ✅ Fixed (3 locations) ✅ Replaced High codecov.yml ✅ Fixed N/A Medium security-analysis.yml ✅ Fixed (3 locations) ✅ Replaced High scorecard.yml ✅ Already compliant N/A Low cifuzzy.yml ✅ Fixed N/A Medium pr-validation.yml ✅ Fixed (1 location) ✅ Replaced Medium reuse.yml ✅ Fixed N/A Low docs.yml ✅ Fixed N/A Medium sbom.yml ✅ Fixed N/A Medium

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
1. Reduced Attack Surface: Least-privilege tokens limit blast radius
  2. Supply Chain Security: SHA pinning prevents action hijacking
  3. MITM Protection: Eliminated download-then-run vulnerabilities
  4. OpenSSF Compliance: Improved Scorecard score (+1.7 points)
  5. Audit Trail: Explicit permissions document workflow requirements
  6. Best Practices: Aligns with GitHub security recommendations

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
1. Maintenance Overhead: Must update SHA pins when updating actions
  2. Mitigation: Renovate automates SHA pin updates
  3. Verbosity: More explicit permissions configuration
  4. Acceptable: Security over brevity
  5. Migration Effort: All 9 workflows required updates
  6. One-time cost: Completed in Sprint 1

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
1. Functional Equivalence: No behavior changes, only security improvements
  2. Python Version Update: Updated MyPy from 3.11 to 3.12 (housekeeping)

docs.title: Token Permission Patterns
docs.text:
Read-Only Jobs (most common): 

permissions: read-all  # Top-level covers all read-only jobs

SARIF Upload (CodeQL, Scorecard, Trivy): 

permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write  # Required for GitHub Security tab

PR Comments (Codecov, Dependency Review): 

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write   # Required for PR comments
  statuses: write        # Required for commit status

GitHub Pages Deployment: 

permissions:
  contents: write  # Required for gh-pages branch update

docs.title: Poetry Installation Pattern
docs.text:
Before (Unsafe): 

- name: Install Poetry
  run: curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -

After (Secure): 

env:
  POETRY_VERSION: 2.1.2

- name: Install Poetry
  uses: snok/install-poetry@76e04a911780d5b312d89783f7b1cd627778900a # v1.4.1
  with:
    version: ${{ env.POETRY_VERSION }}
    virtualenvs-create: true
    virtualenvs-in-project: true

docs.title: Alternative 1: Checksum Verification
docs.text:
run: |
  curl -fsSL -o install-poetry.py https://install.python-poetry.org
  echo "EXPECTED_SHA256  install-poetry.py" | sha256sum -c -
  python3 install-poetry.py
Rejected: More complex, harder to maintain, still network-dependent

docs.title: Alternative 2: Keep Permissive Tokens
docs.text: Rejected: Violates principle of least privilege, fails OpenSSF checks

docs.title: Alternative 3: Mix of Patterns
docs.text: Rejected: Inconsistent security posture across workflows

  • Dangerous-Workflow: 3/10 → 10/10 ✅
  • Pinned-Dependencies: Maintained 10/10 ✅

  • Monthly Review: Verify no new unsafe patterns introduced
  • Security Alerts: GitHub Dependabot for vulnerable actions

docs.title: ADR-005: MkDocs Documentation System with Front Matter Validation
docs.text: Status: ✅ Accepted Date: 2025-11-08 (Implementation), 2025-01-08 (ADR Documentation) Deciders: Byron Williams Related: Documentation Infrastructure, OpenSSF Best Practices

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The project needed comprehensive documentation infrastructure with:

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. User-Friendly: Easy navigation for developers and users
  2. API Documentation: Auto-generated from docstrings
  3. Structured Metadata: Machine-readable documentation metadata
  4. Quality Gates: Validation for documentation standards
  5. SEO: Searchable, discoverable documentation
  6. Compliance: OpenSSF Best Practices documentation requirements
  7. Maintainability: Low-overhead authoring workflow

docs.title: Challenges
docs.text:
1. Mixed Content Types: Guides, API reference, development docs, project docs, security guides
  2. Metadata Quality: Inconsistent front matter across documents
  3. Search Optimization: Need structured data for search engines
  4. Ownership Tracking: Who owns which documentation?
  5. Review Cadence: When was documentation last reviewed?
  6. Automation: How to generate API docs from code?

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Implement MkDocs with Material theme, Pydantic-validated YAML front matter, and automated JSON-LD injection.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
MkDocs (Material Theme)
  ├─ Markdown + YAML front matter (validated by Pydantic v2)
  ├─ mkdocstrings[python] + griffe-pydantic → API from docstrings
  ├─ git-revision-date-localized-plugin → datePublished/dateModified
  ├─ mkdocs-gen-files → build-time Tools Catalog
  ├─ Theme override → global JSON-LD injection from page.meta
  └─ CI Pipeline
       1) Autofix front matter (validate_front_matter.py --fix)
       2) Strict validation (validate_front_matter.py)
       3) MkDocs build --strict
       4) Link checking (lychee)
       5) Deploy to GitHub Pages

docs.title: Key Components
docs.text:
1. MkDocs Material
  2. Modern, responsive theme
  3. Built-in search
  4. Navigation sidebar
  5. Dark mode support

  6. Mobile-friendly

  7. Front Matter Validation (Pydantic v2)

  8. Discriminated unions by schema_type
  9. Required fields: title, description, tags, owner, purpose
  10. Autofix capability for missing/invalid fields
  11. Pre-commit hook integration
---
schema_type: dev  # Discriminator: dev, guide, api, project, security, common
title: "Page Title"
description: "Brief description"
tags: [snake_case, tags]
owner: "core-maintainer"
authors:
  - name: "Byron Williams"
purpose: "One sentence ending with punctuation."
---
  1. mkdocstrings Integration
  2. Auto-generates API docs from Google-style docstrings
  3. griffe-pydantic plugin for Pydantic model documentation

  4. No code imports required (static analysis)

  5. JSON-LD Injection

  6. Structured data for search engines
  7. TechArticle schema for documentation pages

  8. Automatic metadata from front matter

  9. Git-Based Dates

  10. datePublished: First commit of file
  11. dateModified: Last commit of file
  12. Automatic tracking via git-revision-date-localized-plugin

docs.title: Content Organization
docs.text:
docs/
  ├─ index.md              # Project overview
  ├─ guides/               # User guides (7 files)
  │   ├─ installation.md
  │   ├─ quick-start.md

  └─ ADRs/                 # Architecture Decision Records
      ├─ README.md
      ├─ 0001-consolidate-linting-with-ruff.md
      └─ ...

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
1. Professional Documentation: Material theme provides polished, modern UI
  2. Quality Enforcement: Pydantic validation prevents metadata issues
  3. SEO Optimization: JSON-LD structured data improves discoverability
  4. Low Maintenance: Auto-generation reduces manual effort
  5. Ownership Clarity: Front matter tracks document ownership
  6. Automated Validation: Pre-commit and CI enforce standards
  7. API Documentation: mkdocstrings keeps docs in sync with code
  8. Compliance: Satisfies OpenSSF Best Practices documentation requirements

docs.title: ADR-006: Synthetic Validation Dataset Strategy
docs.text: Status: ✅ Accepted Date: 2025-11-05 Deciders: Byron Williams Related: Phase 1 Validation, Quality Assurance Strategy

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The project requires comprehensive validation datasets to verify Image Quality Assessment (IQA) detectors for:

  • Blur detection
  • Skew/rotation detection
  • Noise detection
  • Perspective distortion
  • Contrast assessment
  • Orientation detection

docs.title: Initial Plan
docs.text:
Priority 1 academic datasets identified in DATASET_PRIORITIES.md:

Dataset Purpose Ground Truth Status SOC Dataset Blur/OCR correlation 175 images with Tesseract accuracy ❌ Inaccessible DISEC'13 Skew estimation 1,550 images with precise angles ⚠️ Registration required Kaggle Noisy/Rotated Noise + rotation 1,000+ images ⚠️ API credentials required SignaTR6K Handwriting 6,000+ samples ❌ Unknown availability

docs.title: Accessibility Challenges
docs.text:
Documented in DATASET_ACQUISITION_GUIDE.md:

  1. SOC Dataset: UMD server (lampsrv02.umiacs.umd.edu) returns ECONNREFUSED
  2. Original highest priority (⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ROI)
  3. Only dataset with functional OCR accuracy ground truth

  4. No public mirrors found

  5. DISEC'13: Website requires registration

  6. Dropbox links likely expired

  7. Would require contacting organizers

  8. Kaggle Datasets: Require API setup and credentials

  9. Additional authentication complexity

  10. Privacy/licensing considerations

  11. SignaTR6K: No accessible download found

  12. Paper reference exists but no dataset access

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Immediate Availability: No registration or special permissions
  2. Controllable Parameters: Precise ground truth for threshold tuning
  3. Reproducibility: Deterministic generation for regression testing
  4. Coverage: All IQA dimensions (blur, skew, noise, etc.)
  5. Scale: Generate thousands of validation samples
  6. Maintenance: Actively maintained tooling

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Adopt Microsoft Genalog for synthetic validation data generation instead of academic datasets.

docs.title: Solution Architecture
docs.text:
1. Microsoft Genalog (Primary)
  2. Open-source, actively maintained by Microsoft
  3. Synthetic document degradation engine
  4. Controllable parameters for all IQA dimensions

  5. Supports:

    • Blur (Gaussian, motion, defocus)
    • Skew/rotation (precise angle control)
    • Noise (Gaussian, salt-and-pepper, speckle)
    • Contrast (gamma correction, histogram adjustment)
    • Perspective distortion
    • Morphological transformations

  6. Custom Synthetic Framework (Complementary)

  7. Existing blur/noise/skew generation
  8. Integration with Genalog for comprehensive coverage

  9. Fine-grained control for edge case testing

  10. DocLayNet (Real-World Baseline)

  11. 80,000+ document element annotations
  12. Covers Stage 3B (layout detection)
  13. No IQA ground truth, but real-world complexity

docs.title: Implementation Strategy
docs.text:
# Genalog synthetic generation example
from genalog.degradation.degrader import Degrader

degrader = Degrader([
    ("blur", {"radius": 3}),
    ("bleed_through", {"alpha": 0.5}),
    ("salt", {"amount": 0.01}),
])

degraded_image = degrader.apply_effects(clean_image)

Validation Coverage: - Blur: Gaussian blur with controlled radius (1-20px) - Skew: Rotation with precise angles (-15° to +15°, 0.1° increments) - Noise: Multiple types with controlled intensities - Perspective: Simulated camera angles and lens distortion - Contrast: Gamma and histogram manipulations

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
1. Immediate Availability: No registration, API credentials, or special permissions
  2. Perfect Ground Truth: Exact parameters known (blur radius, rotation angle, etc.)
  3. Reproducibility: Deterministic generation enables regression testing
  4. Scale: Generate unlimited samples for comprehensive coverage
  5. Threshold Tuning: Controlled parameters ideal for calibrating detectors
  6. Maintenance: Microsoft-backed, actively maintained
  7. Cost: Free, no licensing or access fees
  8. Automation: Easily integrated into CI/CD pipeline

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
1. Synthetic Bias: May not capture all real-world degradation patterns
  2. Mitigation: Use DocLayNet for real-world baseline validation
  3. Mitigation: Generate diverse parameter combinations
  4. Domain Gap: Synthetic ≠ real-world scanned documents
  5. Mitigation: Document and monitor false positives/negatives
  6. Mitigation: Incremental real-world testing in production
  7. OCR Correlation: No OCR accuracy ground truth like SOC dataset
  8. Mitigation: Synthetic OCR validation using Tesseract on generated images
  9. Acceptable: Can measure OCR degradation on synthetic samples

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
1. Hybrid Approach: Synthetic + DocLayNet provides comprehensive coverage
  2. Flexibility: Easy to pivot to real datasets if they become accessible

docs.title: Alternative 1: Wait for Dataset Access
docs.text: Rejected: - Blocks project progress indefinitely - No guarantee of eventual access - Registration/permissions may require institutional affiliation

docs.title: Alternative 2: Contact Dataset Authors
docs.text: Rejected: - Time-consuming (weeks to months) - No guarantee of response or access - May require academic collaboration agreements

docs.title: Alternative 3: Use Only DocLayNet
docs.text: Rejected: - DocLayNet has no IQA ground truth - Missing validation for blur, noise, skew, etc. - Stage 3A would be untested

docs.title: Alternative 4: Build Custom Validation Dataset
docs.text: Rejected: - Expensive (manual annotation) - Time-consuming (would delay Phase 1) - Genalog provides superior ground truth

docs.title: Alternative 5: Use Albumentations Library
docs.text: Partially Accepted: - Albumentations provides augmentations, not degradations - Can complement Genalog for additional variations - Not a complete replacement

docs.title: ADR-007: Hybrid IQA Approach for Embedded Images
docs.text: Status: ✅ Accepted Date: 2025-01-15 (Phase 0 Architecture Correction) Deciders: Byron Williams Related: ARCHITECTURE_CORRECTION.md, Phase 0 Foundation

docs.title: Original Architecture (Incorrect)
docs.text:
The initial design assumed a binary fork based on text detection:

Text Detection Gate
    ↓              ↓
[NO TEXT]      [TEXT DETECTED]
    ↓              ↓
IQA Only       Layout Detection Only

Assumption: Documents either contain text OR images, not both.

docs.title: Problem Discovered
docs.text:
Real-world documents (technical docs, academic papers, reports) contain both: - Text: Headers, paragraphs, captions, footnotes - Embedded Images: Diagrams, photos, charts, tables, figures

Critical Gap: The embedded images may have quality issues (blur, low resolution, noise) but were not being assessed.

docs.title: Example Scenario
docs.text: Academic Paper: - Has text (routed to layout detection path) - Contains 5 embedded images (figures) - Figure 3 is blurred (scanned from poor quality photocopy) - Original design: Would detect layout but miss the blur - Impact: Poor OCR quality on Figure 3, degraded downstream processing

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Implement Hybrid IQA: Apply quality assessment to embedded images within text documents.

docs.title: Solution Architecture
docs.text:
Text Detection Gate
    ↓              ↓
[NO TEXT]      [TEXT DETECTED]
    ↓              ↓
IQA on         YOLOv8 Layout Detection
Full Page           ↓
                [Detect All Elements]
                    ↓
                [For Each Image/Figure Element]
                    ↓
                Crop Image Region → Run IQA → Report Quality Issues
                    ↓
                Attach quality_issues to DocumentElement

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Stage 3B Updated: Document Element Detection + Hybrid IQA

# Processing flow
def process_text_document(page_image):
    # 1. Layout Detection (YOLOv8)
    elements = layout_detector.detect(page_image)
    # Returns: tables, images, text blocks, formulas, etc.

    # 2. Hybrid IQA (per image element)
    for element in elements:
        if element.category in [ElementCategory.IMAGE, ElementCategory.FIGURE]:
            # Crop image region
            image_crop = crop_bbox(page_image, element.bbox)

            # Run IQA on cropped region
            quality_issues = iqa_classifier.predict(image_crop)

            # Attach to element metadata
            element.quality_issues = quality_issues
            element.needs_correction = any(
                issue.confidence > CORRECTION_THRESHOLD
                for issue in quality_issues
            )

    return elements

Schema Update: Added quality_issues field to DocumentElement:

class DocumentElement(BaseModel):
    """Detected document element with optional quality assessment."""
    category: ElementCategory
    bbox: list[float]  # COCO format [x, y, width, height]
    confidence: float
    quality_issues: list[DetectedIssue] = []  # Hybrid IQA support
    needs_correction: bool = False
    correction_applied: bool = False

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
1. Comprehensive Quality Assessment: Detects issues in both pure images and embedded images
  2. Targeted Corrections: Apply corrections only to problematic image regions
  3. Text Preservation: Avoids correcting high-quality embedded images unnecessarily
  4. Selective Processing: Can skip corrections on images that don't need them
  5. Accurate Metadata: Per-element quality reporting enables smart downstream processing
  6. Real-World Accuracy: Handles complex documents with mixed content

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
1. Additional Computation: Must run IQA on each detected image element
  2. Mitigation: Only process Image/Figure categories, skip text blocks
  3. Impact: ~2-5ms per image element (acceptable overhead)
  4. Increased Complexity: More complex than binary fork
  5. Acceptable: Reflects real-world document complexity
  6. Bounding Box Dependency: IQA quality depends on accurate layout detection
  7. Mitigation: YOLOv8 achieves 82%+ mAP on DocLayNet

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
1. Schema Change: Required adding quality_issues field to DocumentElement
  2. Pipeline Flexibility: Hybrid approach supports future enhancements

docs.title: Alternative 1: IQA Only on No-Text Path
docs.text: Rejected: - Misses quality issues in embedded images - Fails on technical documentation (most common use case) - Incomplete quality assessment

docs.title: Alternative 2: Run IQA on Full Page Regardless of Text
docs.text: Rejected: - Wastes computation on high-quality text regions - Cannot provide per-element quality reporting - Less actionable for downstream processing

docs.title: Alternative 3: Separate Pipeline for Mixed Documents
docs.text: Rejected: - Adds complexity (3 paths instead of 2) - Harder to maintain - Requires additional routing logic

docs.title: Alternative 4: Skip IQA on Text Documents
docs.text: Rejected: - Unacceptable: Academic papers, reports, manuals contain critical images - Would miss majority of real-world use cases

docs.title: Performance Impact
docs.text:
Before (No Hybrid IQA): - Layout detection: 25-70ms CPU / 2-7ms GPU - Total: ~30ms per text document

After (With Hybrid IQA): - Layout detection: 25-70ms CPU / 2-7ms GPU - IQA per image (avg 3 images): 3 × 8ms = 24ms CPU / 3 × 1ms = 3ms GPU - Total: ~54ms CPU / ~10ms GPU per text document

Overhead: +80% CPU, +40% GPU (acceptable for comprehensive quality assessment)

docs.title: Correction Strategy
docs.text:
# Selective correction based on per-element quality
for element in detected_elements:
    if element.needs_correction:
        # Crop problematic image
        image_crop = crop_bbox(page_image, element.bbox)

        # Apply targeted corrections
        corrected_crop = apply_corrections(image_crop, element.quality_issues)

        # Paste back into page
        page_image = paste_bbox(page_image, element.bbox, corrected_crop)

        # Record correction
        element.correction_applied = True

docs.title: ADR-008: Multi-Stage Pipeline with Text Detection Fork
docs.text: Status: ✅ Accepted Date: 2025-01-15 (Phase 0 Architecture) Deciders: Byron Williams Related: ARCHITECTURE_SUMMARY.md, PROJECT_PLAN.md, Phase 0 Foundation

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text: The system needs to process diverse document types for RAG applications: - Pure images: Photos, scanned images, diagrams (no text) - Text documents: PDFs, scanned pages, reports (with embedded images) - Quality issues: Blur, skew, noise, perspective, contrast - Layout elements: Tables, figures, formulas, handwriting

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Performance: 50-150ms latency per page, 6+ pages/sec throughput
  2. Accuracy: High precision for both IQA and layout detection
  3. Modularity: Independent testing and optimization of components
  4. Maintainability: Easy to upgrade individual components
  5. Cost: Avoid running unnecessary models (performance + compute cost)

docs.title: Key Insight
docs.text:
Different document types require different processing strategies: - Pure images: Need IQA (blur, noise, etc.) but NOT layout detection - Text documents: Need layout detection (tables, figures) AND hybrid IQA on embedded images

Running both on every document wastes 40-60% of computation.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Implement a multi-stage modular pipeline with text detection fork routing documents to specialized processing paths.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Stage 1: Ingestion & Standardization   │
│  • Convert PDF → 300 DPI images         │
│  • Multi-page handling                  │
│  Performance: 30-120ms/page (CPU)       │
└────────────────┬────────────────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Stage 2: Text Detection Gate           │
│  • Ensemble: Morphology + EAST/DBNet   │
│  • Fast routing decision                │
│  Performance: 3-8ms GPU / 20-40ms CPU   │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
               │
        ┌──────┴──────┐
        ▼             ▼
┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
│  NO TEXT     │  │  TEXT DETECTED       │
│  Path A      │  │  Path B              │
└──────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘
        │             │
        ▼             ▼
┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Stage 3A:    │  │ Stage 3B:            │
│ IQA on       │  │ Layout Detection     │
│ Full Page    │  │ + Hybrid IQA         │
│              │  │                      │
│ Classical CV │  │ YOLOv8 → Extract     │
│ + ML Model   │  │ Elements → Per-      │
│              │  │ Element IQA          │
│              │  │                      │
│ 1-3ms GPU    │  │ 2-7ms GPU            │
│ 8-15ms CPU   │  │ 25-70ms CPU          │
└──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────────────┘
       │                 │
       └────────┬────────┘
                ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Stage 4: Correction & Output           │
│  • Apply OpenCV corrections             │
│  • Confidence thresholds                │
│  • JSON metadata generation             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Stage Breakdown
docs.text:
Stage 1: Ingestion & Standardization - Purpose: Normalize all inputs to consistent format - Processing: PDF → 300 DPI PNG images, multi-page handling - Output: Standardized image array per page

Stage 2: Text Detection Gate - Purpose: Fast routing to appropriate processing path - Method: Ensemble (morphological analysis + EAST/DBNet-lite) - Threshold: Calibrated on DocLayNet validation set - Output: Binary decision (text/no-text)

Stage 3A: Image Quality Assessment (No-Text Branch) - Purpose: Assess quality issues in pure images - Methods: Classical CV (Hough, Laplacian, histogram) + ML (CNN) - Issues Detected: Noise, blur, skew, perspective, contrast, orientation - Output: List of DetectedIssue with confidence scores

Stage 3B: Document Element Detection (Text Branch) - Purpose: Detect layout elements and assess embedded image quality - Methods: YOLOv8 layout detection + hybrid IQA - Elements Detected: Tables, images, text blocks, formulas, handwriting - Output: List of DocumentElement with bounding boxes and quality issues

Stage 4: Correction & Output - Purpose: Apply targeted corrections, generate metadata - Methods: OpenCV corrections (deskew, CLAHE, sharpen, denoise) - Output: Corrected images + JSON metadata

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
1. Performance Optimization: Avoid running unnecessary models
  2. Pure image: Skip YOLOv8 layout detection (saves 25-70ms)
  3. Text document: Targeted IQA only on embedded images

  4. Result: 40-60% faster than monolithic approach

  5. Independent Optimization: Each stage can be improved separately

  6. Stage 3A: Swap classical CV for ML without affecting layout
  7. Stage 3B: Upgrade YOLOv8n → YOLOv8s independently

  8. Stage 4: Add new correction methods without changing detection

  9. Maintainability: Clear separation of concerns

  10. Easier debugging (isolate stage failures)
  11. Simpler testing (unit test each stage)

  12. Better code organization

  13. Accuracy: Specialized models for different tasks

  14. IQA model optimized for image quality
  15. Layout model optimized for document structure

  16. Better than single multi-task model

  17. Scalability: Horizontal scaling per stage

  18. Can deploy more workers for bottleneck stages
  19. Different hardware for different stages (CPU vs GPU)

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
1. Complexity: More components to maintain
  2. Mitigation: Clear interfaces between stages, comprehensive testing

  3. Acceptable: Complexity reflects real-world requirements

  4. Text Detection Dependency: Accuracy depends on gate quality

  5. False negative (text→no-text): Miss layout detection
  6. False positive (no-text→text): Waste computation on YOLOv8
  7. Mitigation: Ensemble approach + calibration on DocLayNet

  8. Measured: 95%+ accuracy on validation set

  9. Integration Points: More potential failure points

  10. Mitigation: Error handling at each stage
  11. Fallback: Degrade gracefully (skip stage on failure)

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
1. Pipeline Coordination: Need orchestration logic
  2. Async Opportunities: Can parallelize independent stages (future)

docs.title: Alternative 1: Monolithic Multi-Task Model
docs.text:
Single model predicts quality + layout + elements

Rejected: - 60-100% slower (runs all tasks on every image) - Lower accuracy (multi-task learning trade-offs) - Harder to upgrade (must retrain entire model) - Example: Donut model (good for OCR, poor for IQA)

docs.title: Alternative 2: Three-Way Fork (No-Text, Simple-Text, Complex-Text)
docs.text:
Split text path into simple vs complex

Rejected: - Added complexity without clear benefit - Harder to calibrate decision boundaries - No significant performance gain

docs.title: Alternative 3: Sequential Processing (Always Run All Stages)
docs.text:
Run IQA → Layout → Corrections on every document

Rejected: - Wastes 40-60% computation - Higher latency (50-150ms → 80-250ms) - Higher cost (more GPU time)

docs.title: Alternative 4: Pure Classical CV (No ML)
docs.text:
Use only OpenCV, no deep learning

Rejected: - Lower accuracy for complex issues (noise, perspective) - Misses layout detection entirely - Not competitive with modern systems

docs.title: Text Detection Gate Ensemble
docs.text:
def text_detection_gate(image: np.ndarray) -> bool:
    """Fast text detection using ensemble approach."""
    # Method 1: Stroke density (morphology)
    stroke_score = compute_stroke_density(image)

    # Method 2: Connected components analysis
    component_score = analyze_connected_components(image)

    # Method 3: Edge density
    edge_score = compute_edge_density(image)

    # Ensemble voting
    votes = [
        stroke_score > STROKE_THRESHOLD,
        component_score > COMPONENT_THRESHOLD,
        edge_score > EDGE_THRESHOLD,
    ]

    # Require 2/3 consensus
    return sum(votes) >= 2

Document Type Monolithic Multi-Stage Savings Pure Image 80ms 45ms 44% Simple Text 120ms 75ms 38% Complex Doc 150ms 95ms 37%

Average: 40% faster with multi-stage pipeline

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
def process_document(pdf_path: str) -> DocumentMetadata:
    """Process document through multi-stage pipeline."""
    try:
        # Stage 1: Ingestion
        pages = ingest_pdf(pdf_path)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error("Ingestion failed", error=e)
        raise

    metadata = DocumentMetadata(document_id=pdf_path, pages=[])

    for page_image in pages:
        try:
            # Stage 2: Text Detection
            has_text = text_detection_gate(page_image)

            # Stage 3: Detection
            if has_text:
                elements = detect_layout(page_image)  # 3B
            else:
                issues = detect_quality_issues(page_image)  # 3A
                elements = []

            # Stage 4: Correction (optional)
            corrected = apply_corrections(page_image, issues, elements)

            metadata.pages.append(PageMetadata(...))

        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning("Page processing failed", error=e)
            # Add empty page metadata, continue with next page

    return metadata

docs.title: ADR-009: COCO Bounding Box Format Standardization
docs.text: Status: ✅ Accepted Date: 2025-01-15 (Phase 0 Schema Design) Deciders: Byron Williams Related: schema.py, LayoutParser Integration, Phase 0 Foundation

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Bounding boxes for detected document elements can be represented in multiple formats:

  1. COCO Format: [x, y, width, height]
  2. x, y: Top-left corner coordinates

  3. width, height: Box dimensions

  4. Corner Format: [x1, y1, x2, y2]

  5. x1, y1: Top-left corner

  6. x2, y2: Bottom-right corner

  7. Center Format: [cx, cy, width, height]

  8. cx, cy: Center coordinates
  9. width, height: Box dimensions

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Downstream Integration: System feeds into LayoutParser → Tesseract/Marker/Docling
  2. Interoperability: Common format across object detection frameworks
  3. Validation: Easy to validate (positive width/height)
  4. Compatibility: Must work with YOLOv8, Detectron2, LayoutParser

docs.title: Downstream Tools
docs.text:
LayoutParser: - Accepts: COCO format [x, y, width, height] - Used for: Document layout analysis, reading order detection - Integration: Critical for Phase 3

YOLOv8: - Outputs: COCO format (can convert to others) - Industry standard: MS COCO dataset

Detectron2 (potential future use): - Native: COCO format - Widely used: Facebook AI research framework

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Standardize on COCO format [x, y, width, height] for all bounding boxes.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Schema Definition:

class DocumentElement(BaseModel):
    """Detected document element with COCO-aligned bounding box."""
    category: ElementCategory
    bbox: list[float]  # COCO format: [x, y, width, height]
    confidence: float

    @field_validator("bbox")
    @classmethod
    def validate_bbox(cls, v: list[float]) -> list[float]:
        """Validate COCO bounding box format."""
        if len(v) != 4:
            raise ValueError("Bounding box must have exactly 4 values")

        x, y, width, height = v

        if x < 0 or y < 0:
            raise ValueError("Coordinates must be non-negative")

        if width <= 0 or height <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Width and height must be positive")

        return v

Documentation Standard:

# Example bounding box (COCO format)
bbox = [100.0, 150.0, 250.0, 180.0]
# x=100, y=150, width=250, height=180

# NOT corner format!
# bbox = [100.0, 150.0, 350.0, 330.0]  # WRONG

docs.title: Conversion Utilities
docs.text:
For interoperability with corner-format systems:

def coco_to_corner(bbox: list[float]) -> list[float]:
    """Convert COCO [x, y, w, h] to corner [x1, y1, x2, y2]."""
    x, y, w, h = bbox
    return [x, y, x + w, y + h]

def corner_to_coco(bbox: list[float]) -> list[float]:
    """Convert corner [x1, y1, x2, y2] to COCO [x, y, w, h]."""
    x1, y1, x2, y2 = bbox
    return [x1, y1, x2 - x1, y2 - y1]

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
1. LayoutParser Compatibility: Direct integration without conversion
  2. LayoutParser expects COCO format

  3. Zero-copy integration in Phase 3

  4. Industry Standard: Aligns with MS COCO dataset

  5. Most object detection models output COCO format

  6. YOLOv8, Detectron2, Mask R-CNN all use COCO

  7. Easy Validation: Positive width/height constraints

  8. Negative values invalid (unlike corner format)

  9. Clear semantic meaning (position + size)

  10. JSON Schema Clarity: Self-documenting format 

    {
  "bbox": [100, 150, 250, 180],
  "description": "x=100, y=150, width=250, height=180"
}

  11. Pydantic Validation: Strong typing and validation

  12. Rejects malformed bounding boxes at API boundary
  13. Prevents downstream errors

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
1. Conversion Overhead: Some libraries use corner format
  2. OpenCV: Uses corner format for rectangles
  3. Mitigation: Conversion functions provided, ~1μs overhead

  4. Acceptable: One-time conversion vs. throughout pipeline

  5. Developer Confusion: Must remember format

  6. Common mistake: Using corner format instead
  7. Mitigation: Clear documentation, validation errors, property-based tests
  8. Examples in schema.py docstrings

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
1. Format Choice: COCO vs corner both have pros/cons
  2. Conversion Needed: Some upstream/downstream tools may differ

docs.title: Alternative 1: Corner Format [x1, y1, x2, y2]
docs.text: Rejected: - Incompatible with LayoutParser (requires conversion) - Harder to validate (x2 > x1 and y2 > y1) - Less intuitive for size-based operations - Not COCO standard

docs.title: Alternative 2: Center Format [cx, cy, width, height]
docs.text: Rejected: - Not compatible with LayoutParser - Requires conversion to COCO for YOLOv8 output - Less common in document analysis

docs.title: Alternative 3: Support Multiple Formats
docs.text: Rejected: - Adds complexity (format detection/conversion) - Inconsistent across codebase - Error-prone (which format is this?) - Violates "one way to do it" principle

docs.title: Alternative 4: Normalized Coordinates [0-1]
docs.text: Rejected: - Loses pixel precision - Requires denormalization for cropping - Less intuitive for debugging

docs.title: Property-Based Testing
docs.text:
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

@composite
def bounding_boxes(draw):
    """Generate valid COCO-format bounding boxes."""
    x = draw(st.floats(min_value=0.0, max_value=1000.0, allow_nan=False))
    y = draw(st.floats(min_value=0.0, max_value=1000.0, allow_nan=False))
    width = draw(st.floats(min_value=1.0, max_value=500.0, allow_nan=False))
    height = draw(st.floats(min_value=1.0, max_value=500.0, allow_nan=False))
    return [x, y, width, height]

@given(bounding_boxes())
def test_bbox_format_invariant(bbox: list[float]):
    """Property: COCO bounding boxes must be [x, y, width, height]."""
    assert len(bbox) == 4
    x, y, width, height = bbox
    assert x >= 0
    assert y >= 0
    assert width > 0
    assert height > 0
